newsitem.title: USA: US officials brief families on TWA Flight 800 crash.
newsitem.headline: US officials brief families on TWA Flight 800 crash.

text.p: Families of victims of the crash of TWA flight 800 said on Saturday after briefings by federal investigators that their key questions of what caused the explosion had not been answered.
They said the investigators still did not know whether the Boeing 747, made by Boeing Co was brought down last July 17, killing all 230 people on board, by mechanical failure, bomb or missile.
The National Transportation Safety Board said on Friday that a buildup of volatile vapors in the 747's partially full center fuel tank could have triggered the explosion.
A spoksman for the families of victims, Jose Cremades, said, "The key issues that we wanted to find answers to, have not been answered. Maybe they cannot be answered now."

The board urgently called on the Federal Aviation Administraton to order that steps be taken to assure vapors do not build up to flash point and then for design modifications of the plane to assure against the fuel overheat.
The FAA said it would urgently review the board's recommendations, and Boeing said it would comply with any directives issued by the FAA.

Cremades made his comments after families were briefed by officials of the board, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Navy, whose experts who have so far salavaged more than 90 percent of the plane's wreckage.
TWA's New York-to-Paris flight went down shortly after takeoff.
Cremades said the investigators told the families they had recovered about all of the center fuel tank, "but have not found any evidence of damage by a missile or a bomb."
Asked about recurring theories that it was struck by a missile shortly after takeoff, he said the investigators told them they had found no sign of a missile or bomb.
But, he said, "They are running missile tests in California."
He also said that many of the families were encountering financial hardships since in some cases the main income earner had been killed in the crash.
But he added, "This cannot be blamed on the investigators."
While the board said in its report that evidence from the wreckage was "consistent" with a fuel tank explosion, it stopped short of blaming the crash on mechanical reasons.

It said the cause of the explosion was still open, and it could be mechanical failure, a bomb or a missile, but the tenor of the board's comments and recommendations came the closest yet to ruling out a bomb or missile attack.
However, James Kallstrom, head of the FBI's New York office, took issue with safety board speculation that static electricity caused the explosion.
A spokesman for Kallstrom said, "The FBI position is that it is not helpful to the investigation for either identified or unidentified investigators to be speculating as to the cause of the crash."
About 100 families members attended the briefing in the State Department, one of a series the families have been given since the crash.
An NTSB statement said parts of the wreckage pulled up from the ocean bottom off New York's Long Island showed no evidence that a bomb or missile had brought the plane down.
Instead, it said a reconstruction of the aircraft showed the partially full center wing fuel tank to be deformed "consistent with an explosion originating within the tank."
It said that hot air from the air conditioning units just beneath the tank of Flight 800 might have heated the fuel to flash point temperatures but it was not known what actually led to ignition.
Officials said one of the immediate fixes would be to closely monitor the heat of the fuel in partially full tanks, which tends to rise faster than full tanks, or to fill the tank with an inert gas.
They said a long-term design change would be to require insulation between the tanks and heat generating units, such as the air conditioners.
